------

Slow Road To Fit

Last year’s letter TLDR: I peaked at 252 lbs and started 2023 at an out-of-shape 235 lbs. I lost 30 lbs last year and put on 10 lbs of muscle. Everything about how I ate and exercised changed. The results were slow, but steady.

I said the following in last year’s letter, which is pertinent to the story: “I wanted to try to get off all substances and see how I felt. I had already been off caffeine. Dropped alcohol beyond celebrations. No allergy meds. Not even an Advil when I was sore.”

This year I just kept at it through the first six months of the year and dropped another 5-7 lbs. Then progress started slowing dramatically. At 41, with a demanding career, some unexpected turbulence at work, and four kids, including a baby, it got hard to stay focused. Exercise was steady thanks to the “sweat every day” lifestyle change I’ll tell you about below. But, I hopped on and off the struggle bus with sustaining a 250-500 calorie per day deficit. Experience has taught me that losing weight is a magnitude order more difficult than maintaining.

I tried to understand what was going on and consulted a number of experts. What I learned was that we have two hunger mechanisms that interact: System 1 and System 2. System 1 sets your appetite based on your recent (2-4 days) caloric load and needs. If you overeat in a given period of time, your body nudges you to eat less temporarily. This is why you tend not to over-eat the days following Thanksgiving. The opposite is also true. If you diet, this system is going to rev up. I knew this, as I had experienced it since about day 3 of my journey. In my experience, it’s hard, but straightforward in muscling through it with enough protein and some distractions.

System 2 is more complicated and interacts with System 1. System 2 is a long-term system that adjusts your hunger based on your energy balance over the previous 6-12 months. System 1 is concerned with making sure you can fuel your lifestyle, while System 2 is concerned with you trending towards literal starvation. The more you lose, the more active System 2 gets. If you lose a meaningful amount of body fat, no matter your recent intake, it will override your System 1. This is why body builders coming out of a hard cut are almost uniquely able to put on body fat quickly after the show.

I experienced this phenomenon in a way that shocked me. No matter what I put in my mouth and no matter what combination of protein, fat, and carbs, I couldn’t get rid of this deep ache. It was a constant distraction. And, I naturally ate more in response, slowing or stopping my weight loss. My temporary solution was to exercise more. I started doing at least 90 minutes/day of cardio, and sometimes far more. My body started to hurt all the time, which became its own distraction. And I learned about this delightful phenomena called Exercise Energy Compensation, which still is not fully understood by scientists, but shows that the body can adjust down your non-exercise caloric needs up to 600 calories per day. Said differently, your body will compensate for exercise beyond a point and it’s a waste calorically speaking.

Then one of the doctors I was consulting recommended I try Tirzepatide, which is a dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist and goes by the names Mounjaro or Zepbound. He called it, “a painkiller for hunger.” I laughed and said no. I got on my high horse about not using caffeine, or alcohol, or anything. I had even stopped taking any supplements. This year I’ve had 7 alcoholic drinks, down from approximately 1,000 in 2022. I wasn’t interested in going down that path. Plus I hate – emphasis on hate – needles. He pushed back on me and told me I should start reading the studies on it to make an informed decision. I agreed to start reading up.

As I did, my position softened. It became clear that while there are tradeoffs (side effects) to every decision, the benefit of quieting hunger seemed large and the tradeoffs seemed mild and well-studied at scale. His argument to me was that I had already lost a significant amount of weight by rebuilding my habits, so I was in a far better position to sustain any additional weight loss after going off of it. I was lifting weights consistently and eating high protein, which guards against muscle loss. He said I was an excellent candidate for it to be successful.

I gave it a go, and, well, it worked as advertised. I kept doing what I had been doing, but that deep ache was quieted down. I’m still hungry often, but I’ve stopped thinking about food all the time. In the absence of near-constant pain, my body relaxed. The biggest tradeoff I experienced was in my exercise performance. By keeping your glucose levels within a narrow range, it eliminates your body’s ability to dump glucose into your system during high-intensity exercise. It felt like I lost my 5th gear. Honestly, it sucks, but thankfully I’m not performing for anyone but me.

I broke through 200 lbs, then 190 lbs recently. I’m about 7-9 lbs from my original goal and plan to start coming off tirzepatide soon, which I suspect isn’t easy or straightforward. System 2 will be roaring and I’ll have to readjust to a lower basal metabolic rate. I can’t wait to get my 5th gear back. Although I’m not on social media much these days, I’ll try to share how that’s going.

As an aside, I’m not encouraging anyone to go on Tirzepatide, or any medication. And, I’m certainly not encouraging someone to do so without first renovating their lifestyle, exercise, and eating habits. It’s a powerful tool, but not a magic cure-all. In fact, the body of evidence clearly shows that if you go on these drugs and don’t make lifestyle changes first (lift heavy things, eat plenty of protein), you’ll likely lose a disturbingly large percentage of muscle as your weight loss. This will set you up to be lighter, but far weaker. And, if you regain the weight, you’ll end up at a much higher body fat percentage at the same weight than before you started.

My goal ultimately is both quality and quantity of life, and while this hasn’t always been an enjoyable experience, I believe I am significantly better off where I am than where I started.

What I Learned About Health

I’ve had quite a few people reach out and ask me what I’ve learned along the way. Here’s a short summary in hopes that it helps someone out there who is ready to get started.

Note: I’m a sample size of 1, have no fancy degree in anything including exercise physiology, am not trying to sell you anything, am not sure everything below is completely correct, and didn’t even stay at a Holiday Inn Express last night.

It’s Slow — Unless you’re the first human to break the laws of thermodynamics (which I thought I was for a long time), to lose a pound of fat, you have to under-eat by 3500 calories. And, your body has to preferentially burn all of that as fat, as opposed to muscle, which is rare. A 500 calorie per day deficit is a pound per week. Everything else is water-weight. I’ve found that a deficit of 500 calories per day is about the limit of what can feel sustainably normal. More deficit than that is going to feel hard. I can only do a 750-1000 calories per day deficit for 4-6 days. Then I need a break, even on Tirzepatide.

Lift Heavy, Eat Protein — Assuming you’re in a calorie deficit, to get your body to preferentially burn a higher ratio of fat to muscle requires you to lift heavy things (whatever heavy is for you) and eat plenty of protein. It’s a signal to your body that the most metabolically expensive tissue (muscle) is worth keeping. My experience is that 3 days per week of lifting has gotten great results, but 2 days per week keeps me from losing ground. But, it’s personal. Progressive overload with compound movements has the biggest effect. I aimed to average 180 grams/day of protein (1 gram/day x target body weight), but didn’t always hit it.

Count Calories, Until You Know — II’m allergic to structure and systems, so the idea of counting calories for the rest of my life was a non-starter. But, I did count calories 3 separate times, each for about 3 weeks, and it was revelatory. It’s one thing to know in theory that there are 400 calories in 3 ounces of pistachios. It’s another to grab a small handful of pistachios and realize you just ate 400 calories. Within a short period of time I was able to eyeball my calories in a way that made me conscious of what I was eating and made me realize how frequently I overate.

Measure Glucose, Until You Know — A big part of keeping hunger in check is making sure I don’t spike/crash my blood glucose. I used Levels once for two weeks to eat normally and see how different foods/exercise affected me. The biggest takeaway was how food order seemed to matter (protein first helped a ton) and how much standing or walking affected post-food glucose spikes compared with sitting. I started eating protein first, incorporating a standing desk at work with a treadmill underneath it, and walking whenever I can.

Sweat Every Day — My friend Shane Parrish convinced me that it’s easier to do something 100% of the time than 80% of the time. 23 months ago I decided that I was going to do something active every single day, no exceptions. A 20-minute walk counts. Just be active. Prior to that, I worked out at most once a week, and hated every minute of it. Now my body craves movement.

Quit Negative Self-Talk — I used to joke that I was a “fat kid.” I remember where I was as a 9-year-old when someone called me that, and it stuck. Identity drives behavior. That identity made/allowed me to do stupid stuff like binge eat, because that’s what fat kids do. My friend Patrick lovingly told me to knock it off. He said that’s not who I am and asked me why I kept saying it. I didn’t have a good answer. It was a huge wake-up call.

Cardio Matters, With Caveats — I keep hearing that cardio is a poor way to lose fat, but good for longevity. Also, cardio can burn a lot of calories, but it’s hard outside a lab to measure exactly how many  – and my anecdotal evidence is that fitness trackers considerably over-count. During bouts of long exercise, there’s a gap in expected calories burned and what is practically observed called Exercise Energy Compensation. Bottom line…it’s confusing. Having done a LOT of cardio, here’s where I have landed — 30-60 minutes of hard cardio is an excellent appetite suppressant and helps my body feel much better. Beyond that, it’s still “healthy” but I’ve noticed a compensatory response with hunger that diminishes the fat-loss benefits. I’d build in intense cardio (running, biking, swimming, etc.) a couple times a week and see what you notice.

Supplements, Toxins, Heat/Cold, Red Light Therapy — Over the last couple years I’ve had well-meaning friends recommend all kinds of supplements and techniques that they say helped them, and I’m sure they did. From what I’ve read and observed myself, heat/cold exposure, supplements, and reducing exposure to toxins can and do matter, but they’re the final 5-10%. If you’re focused on these, make sure you’ve already nailed diet, exercise, and sleep.

Sleep Matters — There’s tons of evidence on this. Seems almost like common knowledge at this point. Anecdotally, everything gets easier with good sleep. It’s worth prioritizing. Go dark, cool, and quiet. I use an Eight Sleep and love it.

Fasting Works, But Not How I Expected — You know the quickest way to drop weight? Stop eating. I did quite a few 36-hour fasts, four 3-day fasts, two 5-day fasts, and one 7-day fast. All of them resulted in me feeling food-focused, depleted, and irritable. I lost a little weight, but not as much as expected. My body would get lethargic and stressed. The more research I’ve done, the less I think fasting is beneficial long-term for fat loss, or more precisely, the less I think that the benefits outweigh the costs because of associated muscle loss. But, what fasting did was adjust how I viewed hunger. I realized that not being full isn’t hunger and normal hunger, like skipping a meal, isn’t a big deal or dangerous, and shouldn’t create anxiety.

Seek Support — 2 years of trying to “get fit” felt like an eternity. My hope is that I sustain this for the rest of my life. There’s no way I could have done it for long without friendships, community, and help. But to get help, you have to be vulnerable and honest. Some days I screwed up and gorged myself. Other days I felt terrible and didn’t want to work out. Feeling discouraged is going to come up often. Alex Maples, who recently joined Permanent Equity as our Director of Health and Fitness, has been there every step of the way and deserves a lot of credit.

Grace Not Shame — It took me a long time to gain weight, and I had 40 years of entrenched habits. When I started trying to get fit, I wanted it quick. That led to frustration when my old habits weren’t gone and I couldn’t tell a difference in the mirror. It took a solid year to completely reset my habits, and it has only been recently that people have even noticed that I’ve lost some weight (look up the paper towel roll effect). My advice is to go slow, set low expectations, and just try to get a little fitter every day.

I’m sure I’m wrong on half of this stuff. But, I’d encourage you to eat the fish and spit out the bones. Cheers and hope it's helpful!

Summary

This review article explores the relationship between myosteatosis (the infiltration of fat into skeletal muscle) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Myosteatosis, influenced by aging and overweight, compromises muscle quality and is linked to insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, and cardiovascular risks. Using CT and MRI imaging, researchers have identified distinct fat accumulation patterns associated with metabolic dysfunction.

The review synthesized findings from 10 observational studies worldwide. Evidence consistently showed that individuals with myosteatosis had higher incidence of T2DM, worse glycemic control, increased inflammatory markers, and greater risks of coronary artery disease. Myosteatosis also affects muscle strength and mobility independent of sarcopenia, and it may act as both a marker and driver of insulin resistance.

Despite these associations, the literature highlights major gaps: lack of standardized diagnostic criteria, heterogeneity in methods, and absence of interventional studies. Lifestyle measures (exercise, dietary restriction, weight loss) and emerging therapies (like tirzepatide) show potential in reducing intramuscular fat, but further trials are needed.

---

Highlights

Definition: Myosteatosis is pathological fat infiltration into skeletal muscle, distinct from sarcopenia.

Risk Factors: Aging, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, poor diet, glucocorticoid exposure, and metabolic syndrome.

Pathophysiology:

Ectopic fat deposition impairs insulin signaling.

Inflammatory adipokines (CRP, IL-6, TNF-α) worsen insulin resistance.

Leads to hyperinsulinemia and progression to T2DM.

Clinical Evidence:

Myosteatosis strongly linked to T2DM incidence, insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, coronary calcification, and reduced muscle strength.

Association seen even in non-obese individuals, independent of visceral fat.

Measurement: CT (Hounsfield Units, fat density), MRI (proton density fat fraction), occasionally spectroscopy.

Functional Impact: Leads to early loss of strength and mobility, before loss of muscle mass.

Therapeutic Outlook:

Exercise and hypocaloric diets reduce muscle fat more effectively than diet alone.

Combined interventions (diet + exercise) show most promise.

Novel treatments (tirzepatide, vibration therapy, β-hydroxy β-methylbutyrate) are under study.

Public Health Relevance: Need for standardized diagnostic criteria and interventional studies to guide treatment and prevention.

I think we have an incorrect view of "fatty tissue". This new paper on the topic of "fatty muscle" is a good one (https://t.co/HUf3JaDohx), and while I'm not criticizing it directly,  I think it's reflective of the problematic view. 

Often, when discussing a fatty tissue, such as fatty liver, fatty pancreas, or fatty muscle, we describe the fat as the problem. Something like: "In fatty liver disease, the stored fat promotes insulin resistance". But this isn't the case. 

The fats that are stored in any tissue are triglycerides, which are metabolically inert. They most certainly do not drive any degree of insulin resistance. In fact, the authors of the linked paper above describe the source of this fat, namely "inability of adipocytes to store lipids." In other words, when fat cells are full, they become insulin resistant to prevent further fat storage, and other tissues are forced to pick up the metabolic burden to store more fat. But why does the other tissue store, rather than burn, the fat? Insulin. 

When insulin is elevated and fat cells are "full" (i.e., hypertrophy), other tissues will store fat because they can't burn it. That's the key dynamic: fat cells are "leaking" fats due to ongoing lipolysis, but the elevated insulin forces other tissues to store the fat. If insulin is elevated, fat burning has stopped. 

So, rather than the fat in tissues driving metabolic problems, the stored fat is a symptom of the metabolic problem. It's a sign that fat cells are full and the body is insulin resistant.

There is no direct evidence that GLP‑1 drugs make someone a “better” trader or investor, but there are plausible, material pathways by which they could improve decision quality for certain profiles of market participants—and equally plausible pathways by which they could impair it. The most defensible framing is that GLP‑1 therapies may shift the distribution of trading behaviors by dampening cue‑driven reward pursuit and comorbid behaviors that degrade cognition (alcohol use, poor sleep from untreated OSA, erratic glycemia), while introducing side‑effect risks (fatigue, nausea, anhedonia in a minority, visual safety signals) and potential changes in risk appetite. Net performance impact is likely heterogeneous and state‑dependent: highest upside in traders with obesity or T2D who also contend with cravings, alcohol intake, and sleep fragmentation; lowest or negative in lean, already high‑discipline traders who experience fatigue, blunted reward sensitivity, or mood effects. There are no randomized trials linking GLP‑1s to financial decision‑making per se; conclusions must be inferred from mechanistic and adjacent clinical data.  ￼

Mechanistically, GLP‑1 receptors are expressed in mesolimbic circuits (VTA, nucleus accumbens, septal area) and GLP‑1 agonism modulates dopamine‑linked reward processing. Human neuroimaging and clinical studies show reduced cue reactivity to rewarding stimuli (notably alcohol and palatable foods), and preclinical work demonstrates attenuation of drug‑seeking and conditioned reward. This is consistent with a shift away from immediate reward salience and toward greater top‑down control—not because GLP‑1s are stimulants or nootropics, but because they reduce “wanting” signals that drive impulsive consumption. In an RCT in alcohol use disorder, once‑weekly semaglutide reduced laboratory alcohol self‑administration and craving; an exenatide RCT reduced alcohol cue reactivity and showed exploratory benefits in patients with BMI>30. Large observational datasets also associate semaglutide with lower incidence and recurrence of AUD over 12 months. Translating this to markets, the same circuitry that makes a trader reach reflexively for a drink, snack, or dopamine hit can also propel overtrading, revenge trading, or gambling‑like position sizing; dampening the salience of those urges is directionally favorable for impulse control. That said, the evidence is indirect, and not all reward domains generalize; explicit risk‑taking tasks in humans on GLP‑1s have not been established.  ￼

On “impulsivity” per se, experimental psychometrics distinguish impulsive choice (e.g., steep delay discounting) from impulsive action (inhibitory control). GLP‑1s reliably reduce hedonic drive and cue reactivity, but there are not yet human RCTs showing improved delay discounting or Iowa Gambling Task performance on these drugs. Rodent and primate studies suggest reductions in impulsive choice and drug‑seeking with GLP‑1 agonism, consistent with a broader anti‑consummatory effect, but translating effect sizes to human financial risk behavior is speculative. For a trading desk, the practical read‑through is that some forms of “heat of the moment” decision pressure may subside, but expecting systematic improvements in probabilistic reasoning, risk calibration, or Bayesian updating would be a stretch pending direct data.  ￼

Cognition and vigilance are largely second‑order benefits mediated by comorbidity improvements. In T2D, acute hypoglycemia and high glycemic variability impair attention, processing speed, and executive function; GLP‑1s lower hypoglycemia risk when not combined with insulin or sulfonylureas and improve weight and metabolic parameters, plausibly stabilizing day‑to‑day cognition for diabetic traders. In obesity and OSA, tirzepatide has now demonstrated clinically meaningful reductions in apnea–hypopnea index and improved sleep‑related outcomes, and the FDA approved tirzepatide for moderate‑to‑severe OSA in adults with obesity. Better sleep architecture and oxygenation translate into improved daytime alertness and fewer cognitive lapses—a nontrivial tailwind for intraday trading. Small human studies and reviews suggest potential cognitive benefits (attention, delayed memory, executive function) particularly in insulin‑resistant populations, but findings are mixed and not specific to high‑stakes decision making.  ￼

Distraction load is another relevant channel. “Food noise”—persistent, intrusive thoughts about food—appears to diminish on semaglutide in real‑world surveys and early prospective work, reducing cognitive burden. For traders whose focus is pulled by hunger and cravings, this could translate into more uninterrupted analytical time and fewer micro‑breaks that fragment attention. This research is early, industry‑sponsored in part, and survey‑based; it should be taken as hypothesis‑generating rather than definitive.  ￼

Risks that could degrade trading performance are real and cluster early in titration or at higher doses. Gastrointestinal AEs (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation) are common; fatigue is reported in roughly 5–11% depending on product and trial, and resting heart rate rises on average by 1–4 bpm, both of which can subtly erode resilience during long trading sessions. Delayed gastric emptying can alter the absorption kinetics of oral co‑medications—including extended‑release stimulants—though most formal PK studies show no clinically meaningful effect; monitoring is prudent in individuals using ADHD medication. Mood‑related signals are mixed: some pharmacoepidemiology suggests no increase in suicidality versus comparators, but there are case reports and at least one observational analysis associating semaglutide 1 mg with higher risks of depression/anxiety; causality is not established. Visual safety is an open question. In SUSTAIN‑6, rapid A1c lowering coincided with higher retinopathy complications in diabetics; more recently, multiple cohort studies have raised signals for NAION or neovascular AMD with semaglutide or class use, while others did not confirm increased NAION risk; these are nonrandomized and confounded, but warrant ophthalmic vigilance in older or diabetic users. Any of these issues, if they occur in an individual, can materially impair near‑term trading performance.  ￼

Putting the pieces together for trading behavior, the expected sign and magnitude depend on baseline traits and comorbidities. For a trader with obesity/T2D, frequent nighttime drinking, and probable OSA, GLP‑1 or dual GIP/GLP‑1 therapy could reduce alcohol consumption, improve sleep, stabilize cognition, and reduce cue‑driven impulses—collectively a favorable shift for P&L stability, lower overtrading, and fewer tail‑risk mistakes. For a lean, already disciplined trader without those comorbidities, expected benefits are smaller and risks like fatigue, mild anhedonia, or a subtle downward shift in reward sensitivity might reduce healthy risk‑taking or motivation at the margin. Either way, effects are likely time‑varying: the first 4–8 weeks of dose escalation have the most side effects and the least reliable performance; benefits, where present, accrue as weight loss, sleep improvement, and behavioral changes consolidate over quarters.  ￼

If you want to test this in‑house, the correct approach is an N‑of‑1, pre‑registered protocol rather than anecdotes. Track 24 weeks pre/post initiation with a 4–8 week wash‑in exclusion window. Outcome variables should include turnover, order‑submission latency variance, intraday P&L volatility, stop‑out frequency, realized slippage, overnight gap exposure, drawdown depth and recovery time, daily Sharpe, and error rates on checklists. Complement with digital phenotyping and physiology: actigraphy‑derived sleep metrics, heart rate variability, continuous glucose variability if diabetic, alcohol use days, and validated scales for impulsivity, anhedonia, and mood. Add a 5–10 minute weekly cognitive battery covering inhibitory control and probabilistic learning. Pre‑specify “no trade zone” windows following dose escalations. This is the only way to answer whether the drug’s net effect on that individual’s trading is positive.  ￼

Investment implications extend beyond the individual. First, behavior change spillovers look real in early data. A 2025 RCT and multiple observational studies suggest meaningful reductions in alcohol craving and, in some settings, consumption; combined with reports of dampened food purchasing—particularly snacks and impulse categories—this supports continued relative headwinds for certain alcohol and packaged‑food exposures as GLP‑1 penetration grows. Gambling behavior is biologically plausible as a next‑order effect via reward circuitry, but high‑quality human evidence is limited; position any casino or iGaming thesis on direct data, not mechanism. Second, GLP‑1s’ clinical expansion into sleep apnea (tirzepatide approval; large AHI reductions at 52 weeks) increases persistence, broadens prescriber bases, and strengthens payor arguments, supporting volume durability for the class and suppliers. Third, safety overhangs around vision and mood will drive episodic volatility but are unlikely to be thesis‑breaking absent confirmatory randomized data; nonetheless, they create option value in ophthalmology diagnostics and therapeutics as surveillance intensifies. Finally, productivity‑adjacent benefits—fewer sick days, improved sleep—will surface in macro labor data slowly; they are not a first‑order input to our market models yet, but they argue against a near‑term GLP‑1 reversal narrative.  ￼

Bottom line: GLP‑1 therapy is not a cognitive enhancer, but it can be a behavioral and physiological de‑risking tool whose net contribution to trading quality hinges on the user’s baseline liabilities and tolerance for side effects. For the IC, the rational policy is to treat GLP‑1s as part of a personal risk‑management stack rather than a desk‑wide performance hack: encourage medically indicated use for staff with obesity/T2D or OSA, set clear guidance around scheduling titration away from peak risk periods, and evaluate outcomes with the same rigor we apply to new alpha models. The science supports potential improvements in impulse‑laden behaviors and sleep; it also flags manageable risks that, if ignored, can impair performance. That is a trade worth underwriting thoughtfully, on a case‑by‑case basis.  ￼

Both $ARWR and $WVE are running trials of their INHBE / ALK7 silencers as a monotherapy in obese patients (see attached photos) and so weight loss using INHBE / ALK7 silencers would appear to remain a key objective for the companies. I also think Bruce Givens left $ARWR in 2020.

I think the use of NHBE / ALK7 silencers in formerly insulin resistant / obese patients who have restored metabolic health has a reasonable chance of mirroring the metabolically beneficial effects of the LoF INHBE / ALK7 genetic variants by promoting the maintenance and resilience of a healthy metabolic state, with are some caveats (see note at the bottom). However that is not what the companies' trials are doing. 

You are certainly correct $ARWR (though not $WVE) is testing the silencers in combination with tirzepatide. However, this is not in the context of a maintenance dose following a restoration of metabolic health via GLP-1RAs, which again would make some mechanistic sense. $ARWR is still using its lipolysis stimulating INHBE / ALK7 silencer in obese (or even worse, obese and diabetic) patients of which the vast majority are already suffering from excess adipocyte lipolysis. My sense is that if efficacy is shown in this context it will be because the GLP-1RA was able to get the patient to a healthier metabolic state in-spite of (not because of) the excess lipolysis produced by the INHBE / ALK7 silencers, probably via GLP-1RA stimulating massive increase in insulin which shuts down the activity of AGTL and HSL more than the INHBE / ALK7 silencing stimulates their activity, and then the INHBE / ALK7 silencers were able to exert a beneficial effect once that healthier metabolic state is restored.

In truth, tirzepatide and INHBE / ALK7 silencers are somewhat of a strange combination. Insulin shuts down adipocyte lipolysis, though fails to do so effectively in an insulin resistant state which causes much of the insulin resistance and lipotoxic effects in the surrounding cells. GLP-1 released from the small intestine accounts for 70% of the insulin release from the pancreas in a healthy person. So, GLP-1RAs stimulate massive insulin release. This insulin release acts in exact opposition to what ALK7 and INHBE silencing are doing (just as PPAR-y acts in opposition to ALK7 and INHBE silencers, which makes sense as PPAR-y is an insulin sensitizer). Insulin release inhibits lipolysis by decreasing the quantity and activity of AGTL and HSL, ALK7 / INHBE silencing is increasing the quantity and activity of AGTL and HSL. I can come up with theoretical ways in which inhibiting lipolysis via GLP-1RAs whilst promoting lipolysis via AGTL and HSL behaves synergistically and leads to a positive outcome. However, that's all theoretical musings and my guess is if this approach does work it's not because of the companies' differentiated knowledge about metabolism, or differentiated reasoning about metabolic mechanisms, but pure dumb luck. Though, I think that is an important point. $WVE 's mono or $ARWR 's mono or combo therapies could work due to unknown mechanisms. However, until I see more in-human data (inclusive of MNR or euglycemic-hyperinsulinemia clamp), my view is there is a high probability these therapies will promote a further increase in insulin resistance in patients who are already insulin resistant, and that is a very bad thing for  patients.

Note:  I should say that while I think it is plausible to explore using GLP-1RAs to restore metabolic health and then INHBE / ALK7 silencers to maintain it, and that's probably the best use case for the silencers, I remain skeptical about what will happen with INHBE / ALK7 use in formerly obese patients once the GLP-1RA is stopped. There are latent long-term characteristics seen in formerly obese patients that are not seen in never-obese patients. Many of these differences relate to appetite regulation. The molecular signaling in the formerly obese patient still produces a far stronger appetite drive than in the never obese, which is why weight gain often returns in obese patients once GLP-1RAs are stopped (50-70% regain within a year). If the formerly obese patient returns to his / her former eating habits post INHBE / ALK7 silencer, and there remains molecular predisposition in the adipocyte towards excess lipolysis in the formerly obese (pretty likely), the INHBE / ALK7 silencers are likely going exacerbate that excess lipolysis pretty quickly. You can some see a pre-clinical model of that in the study I posted in my INHBE / ALK7 silencer thread.

An explosive used by the French during WWI, called dinitrophenol (DNP), was also one of the first weight-loss drugs.

DNP is a yellow, musty-smelling chemical. Drying and grinding the mixture released a fine dust that infiltrated the lungs of munitions workers. One French artillery maker, named Georges, was found dead; his skin dripping with yellow-tinged sweat and his temperature at 43 Celsius.

Between 1916 and 1918, several dozen workers died like this in French factories. A person investigating the deaths, named Roger Perkins, noted: “Workers claim that they have grown thin to a notable extent after several months’ work in DNP.” This observation would spur one of the first weight loss drug crazes.

In 1931, Stanford doctors found that daily DNP increased metabolic rate by 40 percent and caused an average loss of 0.9 kg per week. Within a year, they had supplied over 1,200,000 capsules—enough to treat 4,500 patients—and estimated at least 100,000 Americans had taken it.

Unlike many other weight loss drugs of the era, DNP actually worked, but it could kill even at prescribed doses. In 1934, Time reported two sudden deaths, including a young woman in Los Angeles who “followed directions on the box and died violently within a week.” In 1938, the FDA banned DNP; other countries followed. Today, it’s mostly forgotten outside niche bodybuilding circles, replaced by safer drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro.

DNP increases metabolism by acting as a “mitochondrial uncoupler,” destroying the proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis. This forces energy to be burned as heat, prompting mitochondria to burn more fat and glucose to compensate. If the dose is too high, body temperature rises uncontrollably.

The new warning on the Ozempic label states that:

Ileus: Ileus is a serious but rare side effect that has been reported in patients taking Ozempic. Ileus can cause abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and constipation. If you experience any of these symptoms, contact your healthcare provider immediately.

The FDA also recommends that healthcare providers monitor patients taking Ozempic for signs and symptoms of ileus, and that they consider discontinuing Ozempic if ileus is suspected.

The point being underscored here is that we have a drug on the market, but the risks of the drug are far from nailed down.

The Focus of Every Ozempic Lawsuit Is the Failure to Warn
Every Ozempic lawsuit asserts the key claim in this litigation: Novo Nordisk, the maker of Ozempic, failed to provide adequate warnings about the risk of developing gastroparesis, a condition characterized by delayed stomach emptying, as a side effect of the drug.

While the Ozempic label mentions common adverse reactions like nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and constipation, it does not link these symptoms to gastroparesis, nor does it include them in the “Warnings and Precautions” section. The label does mention delayed gastric emptying in the context of drug interactions. It describes a minor delay in gastric emptying as part of the drug’s mechanism. Still, it does not explicitly state gastroparesis as a risk or potential chronic condition resulting from Ozempic use.

Additionally, Novo Nordisk’s promotional materials, including their primary website, fail to mention the risk of gastroparesis in the “Important Safety Information” section. The materials also highlight changes in labeling over time, such as the removal of specific guidance on side effects from the “Patient Counseling Information” section, which may cause physicians to misinterpret symptoms like vomiting as minor or temporary.

Victims’ Ozempic lawyers argue that Novo Nordisk was aware or should have been aware of the potential link between Ozempic and gastroparesis, based on clinical studies, case reports, and medical literature. That is the core of these lawsuits. The company failed to provide adequate warnings about this risk, which allegedly led to a lack of awareness in the medical community and potentially affected prescribing decisions.

You also have to remember that we are not just talking about Ozempic in terms of clues to the risk. Ozempic is a GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA). The risk of gastroparesis is common across the GLP-1RA class, which includes medications like tirzepatide, exenatide, liraglutide, albiglutide, dulaglutide, and lixisenatide. Published literature on the association between gastroparesis and any GLP-1RA, not just Ozempic, should have alerted manufacturers to the need for warnings about this risk to patients and prescribing physicians.

Ozempic lawsuits contend that if the risks of gastroparesis had been adequately disclosed, it would have influenced the physician’s decision to prescribe Ozempic or to monitor for symptoms of gastroparesis more closely. Why not disclose the risk? There could be any number of reasons. But, like everything, it usually comes down to money. More warnings equal fewer sales, which equals less money. Ozempic Class Action Lawsuit
In February 2024, the MDL panel certified an Ozempic class action lawsuit. A Multidistrict Litigation (MDL) class action can potentially speed up the settlement process in lawsuits like the Ozempic case in two important way that may lead to earlier Ozempic settlements:

Streamlined Proceedings: MDLs consolidate similar cases to streamline the legal process. By bringing numerous similar lawsuits under one court, MDLs help reduce duplicative discovery, avoid conflicting rulings in different courts, and increase the efficiency of the legal process. This consolidation can lead to quicker settlements because it creates pressure on the defendants to resolve many cases at once rather than dealing with each case individually over a prolonged period.

Higher Negotiation Leverage: In an MDL, the large number of cases consolidated together increases the plaintiffs’ negotiation leverage. This can encourage the defendant, in this case, Novo Nordisk, to settle to avoid the risk of facing a potentially large, cumulative judgment across many individual cases. Settlements in an MDL can offer compensation to claimants more quickly than individual lawsuits, which might take years to resolve. Ozempic settlement amounts are unlikely to be one-size-fits-all. If these claims are successful, Ozempic settlement payouts will vary depending on the severity of the side effects and the evidence supporting the plaintiffs’ claims.

Our lawyers sometimes refer to the Ozempic MDL (multidistrict litigation) as a class action lawsuit because that is what people call it (and, frankly, how they search it), but it is important to understand that these two legal mechanisms are distinct.

Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) — Comprehensive Bullet Notes

---

1. Definition & Pathogenesis

Functional collapse of the pharyngeal airway during sleep → recurrent apneas (≥ 10 s airflow cessation) or hypopneas (≥ 30 % flow reduction + arousal or ≥ 3 % desaturation). 

Negative inspiratory pressure, reduced neuromuscular tone, and structural narrowing (obesity, retrognathia, tonsillar hypertrophy) combine to exceed critical closing pressure (Pcrit), driving obstruction.

Intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation trigger sympathetic surges, oxidative stress, and systemic inflammation—the root of cardiovascular and metabolic sequelae.

---

2. Key Clinical Features

Night-time clues

Loud habitual snoring, often punctuated by witnessed breath holds and gasping arousals.

Fragmented sleep, nocturia, diaphoresis, restless sleep, GER symptoms.

Day-time clues

Excessive sleepiness, non-refreshing sleep, morning headaches, dry mouth, poor concentration, mood disturbance.

Treatment-resistant hypertension, central obesity (BMI > 30 kg m²), and neck circumference > 40 cm are strong phenotypic flags. 

---

3. Screening & Diagnostic Criteria

Screening questionnaires: STOP-Bang ≥ 3, Berlin “High risk”, or Epworth ≥ 10 warrants formal testing.

Gold standard: Full-night attended polysomnography scoring airflow, respiratory effort, oximetry, arousals, limb leads, and EEG. 2025 AASM statement reinforces arousal-based hypopnea scoring for accuracy. 

Home sleep apnea test (HSAT): endorsed for uncomplicated adults when PSG access is limited; must record at least airflow, oximetry, and effort. 

Apnea–Hypopnea Index (AHI) defines severity:

Mild: 5–14 events/h

Moderate: 15–29 events/h

Severe: ≥ 30 events/h

ICSD-3-TR diagnostic criteria (any of the following):

AHI ≥ 5 with symptoms/signs OR

AHI ≥ 15 regardless of symptoms. 

---

4. Medical (Non-surgical) Management

Weight optimisation

≥ 10 % weight loss can halve AHI; include evidence-based programmes (dietician + exercise). 

Tirzepatide (Zepbound) now FDA-approved for OSA in obese adults; Medicare/Medicaid coverage from 2025. 

Positive airway pressure

Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) is first-line; titrate in-lab or use auto-adjusting devices.

Bilevel PAP considered for pressure-intolerant patients or those with overlap COPD.

Adherence strategies: mask fitting, humidification, behavioural coaching, telemonitoring.

Mandibular advancement devices

Custom, titratable oral appliances indicated for mild-to-moderate OSA or CPAP refusal/intolerance.

Adjunctive measures

Positional therapy for supine-predominant OSA.

Nasal corticosteroids or decongestants if nasal obstruction drives pressure intolerance.

Avoidance of alcohol, sedatives, and sleep deprivation.

Oxygen or acetazolamide in select central-mixed phenotypes after specialist review.

---

5. Surgical & Device-Based Management

(consider after CPAP failure or anatomic candidacy; 2025 AASM guideline provides referral triggers) 

Upper airway soft-tissue surgery

Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) ± tonsillectomy for retropalatal collapse.

Lateral pharyngoplasty or Barbed reposition pharyngoplasty offers better airway widening with less fibrosis.

Transoral robotic tongue-base reduction (TORS) or radiofrequency ablation for glossal hypertrophy.

Skeletal surgery

Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA) advances facial skeleton ~10 mm, expanding airway; success highest in severe, craniofacial narrowing.

Hypoglossal nerve stimulation

Implantable system senses inspiration and advances the tongue; indicated when BMI < 32 kg m², AHI 15–65, and no concentric collapse on drug-induced sleep endoscopy.

Nasal surgery (septoplasty, turbinate reduction) improves PAP tolerance rather than cures OSA.

Tracheostomy remains a life-saving option in severe refractory OSA or when other therapies are contraindicated.

Based on the patent’s examples, a representative sequence is that of Compound 10 (SEQ ID NO: 20), which is one of the compounds with detailed potency data. Its full sequence in one-letter code (with Aib denoted as X for consistency with patent notation) is:
YXEGTFTSDYSILLEEQAAREFIEWLLAGGPSSGAGQAPGQAPGASHLSTAQTQRLSAELHKLATLPRTETGSGSP-NH2
•  Substituting X for Aib (2-aminoisobutyric acid, a non-natural amino acid for stability): YAibEGTFTSDYSILLEEQAAREFIEWLLAGGPSSGAGQAPGQAPGASHLSTAQTQRLSAELHKLATLPRTETGSGSP-NH2
•  Length: ~75 amino acids (C-terminal amidation for stability).
•  Structural breakdown:
•  Z1 (GLP-1/GIP domain, positions 1–34, based on SEQ ID NO: 1 variant): YAibEGTFTSDYSILLEEQAAREFIEWLLAGGPSSG (similar to tirzepatide but with substitutions for optimized tri-activity).
•  L1 (linker, positions 35–46): AGQAPGQAPG (one of several possible linkers from Table 2, e.g., SEQ ID NO: 136; others include E, GE, APPPSGGGE, etc., to separate domains and maintain folding).
•  Z2 (amylin domain, positions 47–77, based on SEQ ID NO: 2 variant): ASHLSTAQTQRLSAELHKLATLPRTETGSGSP-NH2 (a modified amylin/calcitonin hybrid for receptor selectivity).
•  Lipidation: Attached to the epsilon-amino group of the lysine (K) at position 63 (within the Z2 domain, in the “HKL” motif), using a C20 diacid-gammaGlu-2xAdo moiety (Chem. 27) or similar (e.g., C18 diacid variant, Chem. 28). This is analogous to tirzepatide’s lipidation but positioned in the amylin domain for some variants to balance pharmacokinetics.
Other examples like Compound 52 (SEQ ID NO: 62) are highly similar, with minor substitutions in Z1 or Z2 (e.g., YAibEGTFTSDYSILLEEQAAREFIEWLLAGGPSSGAGQAPGQAPGASHLSTAQTQRLSAELHKLATLPRTETGSGSP-NH2) and lipidation potentially at a different K (e.g., position 33 in Z1).

Alignment and differences of tirzepatide with the tri-agonist (using Compound 10 as representative):
•  Shared N-terminal motif (YAibEGTFTSDYSI…): Both start identically up to position 12, reflecting GIP/GLP-1 homology for receptor binding.
•  Mid-sequence divergence: Tirzepatide has AibLDKIAQ[K]AFVQWLIAGG (positions 13–28, with lipidated K at 20 and exendin-4-like tail for GLP-1 potency). The tri-agonist has LLEEQAAREFIEWLLAGG (positions 13–28), with substitutions (e.g., L13 vs. Aib13, EEQ vs. DK I, REFIE vs. AFVQ) to accommodate tri-activity while maintaining dual agonism. No lipidated K in this region for the tri-agonist—instead, it’s shifted to Z2.
•  C-terminal extension: Tirzepatide ends with PSSGAPPPS-NH2 (exendin-4-derived for stability/potency). The tri-agonist replaces this with PSSG + linker (AGQAPGQAPG) + amylin domain (ASHLSTAQTQRLSAELHKLATLPRTETGSGSP-NH2), adding ~36 residues for amylin receptor engagement. This makes the tri-agonist ~2x longer, potentially altering pharmacokinetics but enabling triple agonism in a single chain (vs. co-administration of dual + amylin agonists).
•  Overall similarity: ~50–60% identity in the overlapping GLP-1/GIP domain, with the tri-agonist engineered as a fusion peptide to incorporate amylin activity without conjugating separate molecules (as in some reference compounds in the patent, which showed potency loss).

Key Differences Between HFCS and "Normal" Sugar
HFCS: A liquid sweetener derived from corn, commonly used in processed foods (e.g., sodas, cereals, sauces). It's typically 55% fructose and 45% glucose, which can lead to faster absorption and potentially greater metabolic effects like insulin resistance or liver fat buildup.
Sucrose ("Normal" Sugar): Table sugar from cane or beets, composed of 50% fructose and 50% glucose. It's often used in home cooking, baked goods, and some beverages.
Both are added sugars with similar caloric content, but HFCS is more prevalent in ultra-processed, hyper-palatable foods, which may make it more susceptible to GLP-1 effects.
Impact of GLP-1 Medicines: HFCS vs. Sucrose
GLP-1 drugs don't discriminate between sugar types at a molecular level—they reduce overall desire for sweet, high-calorie foods by acting on the brain's reward centers (e.g., via dopamine pathways) and slowing digestion. However, patterns emerge based on where these sugars are found:

What if a heart attack and lifetime of statin drugs could be avoided with a one-time, two-hour infusion?

Kiran Musunuru, a University of Pennsylvania cardiologist and leading gene-editing researcher, thinks it’s possible.

Musunuru cofounded Verve Therapeutics, a company developing a therapy that uses gene editing to essentially turn off one of the liver genes that produces LDL, or bad cholesterol.

Eli Lilly in June announced plans to acquire Boston-based Verve for up to $1.3 billion.

The deal is a sign that one of the largest pharmaceutical companies, known for its blockbuster diabetes and weight-loss drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound, sees promise in genetic therapies like Verve’s.

Musunuru is not employed by Verve, which he helped to found in 2018, but serves as a scientific adviser and has a financial stake in the company. At Penn, he remains deeply entrenched in advancing the science powering Verve’s therapy.

The approach uses CRISPR, a gene-editing technology that allows scientists to alter DNA. It is named after a stretch of genetic code utilized — “Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats.”

CRISPR works like a biological find-and-replace tool, and can be programmed to find a specific irregularity within a strand of DNA, then cut it out or replace the incorrect letter.

Musunuru and colleagues at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia recently published the outcome of a landmark case in which they developed a custom CRISPR treatment for an infant, named Baby KJ, who was born with a rare metabolic disorder that prevented him from processing protein.

The Penn and CHOP team designed KJ’s CRISPR treatment to find and correct a genetic misspelling in a liver enzyme.

Their success captured international attention for its potential to treat rare disorders. But Musunuru says CRISPR’s potential is much broader.

Heart disease has become a leading cause of death, and Musunuru thinks it could be addressed with a two-hour CRISPR infusion.

“Why are we waiting for someone to have a heart attack?” he said. “What if you give them a one-time treatment and their cholesterol levels are permanently lower?”

The Inquirer spoke to Musunuru about what’s next for CRISPR technology.

How could CRISPR be used for heart disease?

The therapy embeds CRISPR components into lipid nanoparticles — essentially tiny soap bubbles — that are infused into the bloodstream.

The nanoparticles also contain mRNA, a type of genetic molecule that acts as a GPS to guide the CRISPR components to their target, a liver gene that produces so-called bad LCL cholesterol.

“We give it a 20-letter address, the location in a cholesterol gene,” Musunuru said.

The nanoparticles are naturally absorbed by the liver, taking advantage of the liver’s job, which is to filter blood.

Once in the liver, the CRISPR components are released and begin to search for their target cholesterol gene, and switch it off.

In an early clinical study, a patient in his 20s with a severe high cholesterol condition saw his bad cholesterol rate drop by 60% and remain low for two years.

What’s the benefit of a one-and-done treatment for high cholesterol?

Statin medications are widely used to help control cholesterol and reduce the risk of heart disease. But research has found that people who are prescribed the medication after a heart attack often don’t stick with the drug, which must be taken daily.

What’s more, the treatment could one day be given to people who are known to be at high risk of developing heart disease, potentially avoiding a heart attack.

A two-hour infusion that eliminates the need for a daily medication could be especially beneficial in developing countries that lack access to healthcare or depend on outside sources to supply medications, since that supply can be unreliable.

What’s next for Verve?

Eli Lilly announced plans in June to acquire Verve for up to $1.3 billion.

Musunuru said he hopes the pharmaceutical giant’s support will accelerate the development of Verve’s cholesterol drug.

The drug is still years away from potentially becoming available. It needs more clinical testing to prove it is safe and effective, and must complete a rigorous regulatory approval process.

How else could CRISPR be used?

So far, researchers have had the most success using CRISPR to treat blood disorders (like sickle cell disease) or diseases associated with the liver. These are easy targets for CRISPR technology, since the therapies are infused into the bloodstream and are readily filtered by the liver.

The first Food and Drug Administration-approved CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease works by turning off a gene that causes red blood cells to become misshapen.

Breast and ovarian cancers associated with BRCA gene mutations could be a potential next target.

Researchers have found that ovarian cancer typically begins in the fallopian tubes, which are relatively accessible organs because they are closer to the body’s surface. Breast cancer often begins in breast ducts, also close enough to the surface of the body.

Scientists are exploring whether a CRISPR solution injected directly into the fallopian tubes or breast ducts could potentially shut off the mutated gene before it causes cancer.

People with BRCA gene mutations have such a high risk of developing cancer that many preemptively opt to have their breasts or ovaries removed. Being able to “turn off” the cancer-causing gene could dramatically reduce their risk and the need for such drastic preventive measures.

@📌 Key Takeaways:

Metabolic hypogonadism in obese men is an underdiagnosed but clinically significant condition, closely linked with insulin resistance and increased diabetes risk.

Tirzepatide (TZP), a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist, was associated with robust improvements in body composition and gonadal hormones over 2 months: 

Significant reductions in weight, waist circumference, binge eating scores (BES), and fat mass.

Improvements in total and bioavailable testosterone (TT), LH, FSH, and SHBG.

Greater benefits than lifestyle interventions alone or transdermal testosterone replacement.

Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) corrects hypogonadism but does not address underlying obesity and insulin resistance.

Tirzepatide may "restore" endogenous hormonal function, potentially breaking the vicious cycle of obesity → insulin resistance → hypogonadism.

💡 Clinical Insights:

✅ Why does this matter?

Obesity suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis, resulting in low testosterone.

Restoring testosterone without treating obesity perpetuates underlying metabolic dysfunction.

TZP addresses both metabolic derangements and hypogonadism.

✅ Possible mechanisms:

Weight loss and reduction in visceral adiposity may relieve suppression of the HPG axis.

Unclear if tirzepatide exerts direct action on HPG axis independent of weight loss — warrants further mechanistic studies.

✅ Patient selection:

Ideal candidates: Men with obesity-related functional hypogonadism not seeking fertility.

Caution: Study excluded patients on common comorbidity medications (e.g., antihypertensives, statins, antidiabetics), so results may not generalize broadly yet.

🔔 Critical limitations:

Small, non-randomized pilot study (n=83, 2-month duration).

No placebo group.

Durability and long-term safety need confirmation before routine clinical adoption.

Not powered to determine direct versus weight-loss-mediated effects.

📝 Practice Implications:

🔹 Lifestyle modification remains first-line for obesity-related hypogonadism.

🔹 Tirzepatide may emerge as a preferred metabolic-hormonal rebalance strategy if larger, long-term studies confirm benefits.

🔹 TRT should not be used reflexively in obese hypogonadal men — address weight and insulin resistance first.

✅ Conclusion:
Tirzepatide offers a novel, potentially disease-modifying approach for functional hypogonadism in obese men, superior to TRT alone, but should be used cautiously pending larger randomized trials.

Diabetics who rapidly get their blood sugar under control have been found to be at an increased risk of early worsening of diabetic retinopathy.

I've noticed this has confused some people recently.

Firstly, here's what I mean by having blood sugar under versus out of control. The person on the top mostly has their blood sugar in the safe range; that's "good" glucose control. The person on the bottom is going out of range all the time and has generally higher blood sugar; that's "poor" glucose control.

A few studies have found that people with diabetic retinopathy at baseline, who then gain glycemic control, have high risk of retinopathy. Here's a dramatic example from a review:

Those patients underwent intensive insulin treatment and diabetic retinopathy followed at pretty high rates. The reason why is not super clear, and if you read other literature, you might come away expecting the opposite. For example, there's a Cochrane review on the subject of intensive versus conventional treatment, and it suggests that intensive therapy is likely to be beneficial, with some possibility for short-term harm and longer-term benefit:

Getting glycemic control rapidly can definitely do both things—that is, it can be both good and bad for different outcomes and for different people. The confusion is about whether the good or the bad apply to you.

I've noticed lots of people confused recently about claims related to retinopathy after starting to use GLP-1RAs. Well, those do result in glycemic control coming about extremely rapidly, so, like insulin, they're likely to be a risk for those who are at-risk.

A recent study* looked at this with tirzepatide and found that there was no elevation in risk for retinopathy progression or maculopathy, but there was an increase in the risk of proliferative retinopathy. But, at the same time, there was reduced risk of developing any retinopathy among those who didn't have it already.

These results were found in a sample with type-2 diabetes, but among the people in that sample, risk still differed by baseline retinopathy status. For type-2 diabetics without issues at baseline, and very likely for individuals who are also fine at baseline but not diabetic, it's probable that tirzepatide is protective. But for type-2 diabetics who don't know their risk, they might end up hurt by the drugs, justifying an ophthalmology visit before starting.

The issue I keep seeing with interpreting results like these is to take the results for at-risk diabetics and to generalize them to the whole population. That confusion seems to be the source for a lot of kvetching about GLP-1RA-related risks that simply don't exist and might even be reversed for most people.
